raw_response.printed_headline_estimate: Phase I (1870-1884) annual infant mortality rate (IMR): civilian = 171.6 vs military = 156.5 per 1,000 live births, Kolmogorov-Smirnov two-sample test KS = 0.730, n = 15 years, p = .66 (secular trend Spearman rs = .557, df = 13, p = .031); Phase II (1885-1899) IMR: civilian = 160.4 vs military = 124.2 per 1,000 live births, KS = 1.461, n = 15 years, p = .028 (Spearman rs = -.207, df = 13, p = .459) (PDF p. 6 / journal p. 404; underlying counts in Note 29, PDF p. 27 / journal p. 425).
raw_response.publication_year_note: Printed on PDF p. 1 as Journal of Family History, Vol. 27 No. 4, October 2002, pp. 399-429 (2002 Sage Publications); no separate online-first date is printed.
raw_response.rationale: The full text reports inferential statistics—specifically Kolmogorov-Smirnov two-sample tests and Spearman rank correlations on 15-year annual series comparing military and civilian populations in Phase I (1870-1884) and Phase II (1885-1899)—so it is not purely descriptive. However, the sole outcome tested inferentially is the infant mortality rate (deaths under age one per 1,000 live births), which is a downstream health/mortality indicator rather than a Criterion 4 household or community water/sanitation service access outcome. All data on differential water/sanitation governance and access—such as military daily gallon rations, systematic military tank inspections, Governor Adye's prohibition on imported Spanish well water, free condenser water for military families versus a price of six gallons per penny for civilians, and 1878 civilian patio shares with cisterns (39.9%), wells (29%), or neither (40%)—are presented strictly as descriptive historical figures without inferential statistical tests on a water or sanitation access outcome.
